sketch.caption: The piece funnels from background and method into a long spine of eyewitness-case groups, which converge into a statistical synthesis and a set of benchmark cases, then close on a call for coordinated research.

scenes.title: Overview

items.text: 'Ball lightning' coined, but field stays unproven
Rare on camera — so compile expert eyewitness reports
Haidinger's 1868 Vienna multi-sighting
Marsh, Bellido and early professional witnesses
Gerlach, Durward, Dolezalek: speed & damage calculations
Breitenecker, Jennison, Dmitriev: motion and ozone traces
More cases: Mickelson to Wustinger & Kuzmin
Childhood sightings of later scientists (e.g. Wittmann)
Weather observers & coastguards (Pikes Peak to Fishguard)
Amateur astronomers, military, business witnesses
41 cases: thunderstorm-timed, but sizes & behavior vary widely
Richmann, Charcot's patient D-cy: myth vs. medical record
Dorstone, Poughquag, modern spectroscopy & field tests
Call for coordinated, evidence-based ball lightning research

items.text: LEGEND & MEDICAL RECORD
PHYSICAL EVIDENCE
Richmann (1753): popular 'ball lightning' myth, actually ordinary lightning
Charcot's patient D-cy (1889): keraunoparalysis vs. lasting traumatic neurosis
Dorstone tub (1936): energy estimate from boiled water
Poughquag glass door (2008): fluorescence measurement
Uman's triggered-lightning field tests (2008)
Cen (2012) & Nikitin (2015): spectra and video triangulation
Both kinds of case anchor theory-testing against reality

plates.title: The Chain of Witnesses
plates.prompt: An illuminated manuscript leaf on aged cream parchment, sepia ink linework with muted gold, red-ochre and blue pigment washes, bordered by a thin gilt rule and no other ornament. Read top to bottom as a single chain of small framed medallions joined by delicate painted gold pathways, each medallion a complete little scene with its title lettered in small roman capitals directly beneath it, and no other words anywhere on the page. At the top, BUTTI'S FIREBALL, MILAN 1841: a man at a window over a rainy street crowd beneath a reddish-yellow fireball. A path leads down to 12,000 PHOTOGRAPHS, TWO BALLS: a robed figure poring over trays of small night-sky photographic plates. From this a path enters a large gilt-bordered enclosure labelled by its drawn contents alone (no caption) holding five medallions in a vertical sequence joined by connecting lines: HAIDINGER'S WINDOW BALL, 1868 (a man at a window watching a glowing ball hover outside the pane); GERLACH CALCULATES THE SPEED (a scholar with chalk and diagram tracing a ball's straight path across the sky); WITTMANN'S CHILDHOOD SPHERE, 1951 (a boy in a doorway watching a yellow-white ball sink into a tree); PIKES PEAK WOODSHED BALL (a mountain-station worker in a woodshed as a ball passes through); BAGNALL'S BEDSIDE ORB, 1974 (a man sitting up in bed watching an orange sphere hover near a window). Lines from the last two medallions converge beneath the enclosure into SIZES FROM 1.5 CM TO 15 M: an unrolled measuring scroll showing circles of greatly different sizes. From this convergence point two gold paths fork into a second, smaller gilt enclosure holding two side-by-side medallions: RICHMANN'S LEGENDARY BALL, 1753 (an engraved-looking scene of a man struck by a dramatic fiery sphere) and DORSTONE'S BOILING TUB, 1936 (a red-hot ball falling toward a wash-tub beneath a cottage window). Both paths descend and meet at the bottom in the final medallion, BUILDING THE SHARED DATABASE: robed scholars at a table laying photographs and notes into one open ledger. Keep the whole composition tall and narrow in the visual chain but let each medallion be wide enough to read clearly, with generous bare parchment around the frames rather than crowding them.

plates.title: Inside the Chain: Scientists at the Window
plates.prompt: The same illuminated parchment leaf, sepia ink and muted gold-red-blue wash, bordered by a single gilt rule, no words anywhere except the small roman-capital titles lettered beneath each medallion. This plate opens with the identical medallion that marked the scientists' enclosure in the overview page, now set at the top as the doorway into this section: HAIDINGER'S WINDOW BALL, 1868, a man at a window watching a ball hover outside the pane. Below it the page divides into two parallel columns of medallions joined by thin gold threads, like two chains of beads running down the leaf and meeting at the bottom. Left column, reading downward: LIGHTNING'S STRONG RAMIFICATIONS (a forked bolt striking down toward a horizon, seen from a window); BALL THROUGH THE MORTUARY WALL (a fist-sized blue-white ball gliding across an old mortuary floor toward an open door); OZONE IN THE BALL'S TRAIL (a figure on a river raft holding glass sample-bulbs up to a smoky trail in the air); MOSCOW'S BLUE JELLYFISH, 1997 (two onlookers on a bridge watching a soft blue sphere drift past their faces). Right column, reading downward beside it: FIREBALL STRIKES THE DECK (a pink ball exploding on a ship's deck, knocking a sailor down); SPHERE DOWN THE AIRCRAFT AISLE (a glowing sphere drifting down a lit aeroplane cabin aisle past a seated passenger). The two gold-thread columns bend inward near the foot of the page and both arrive together at a single larger medallion at the very bottom: SPHERE BREAKS INTO TWELVE, showing a falling plasma ball shattering above a treetop into a dozen smaller glowing spheres scattering toward a wet road. Keep every medallion large enough that the small figures and lightning within it are legible, spacing them generously down the full height and width of the leaf rather than crowding a narrow central strip; the parchment should show bare space between the two columns and around the converging point at the bottom.

plates.title: Legend and Physical Trace
plates.prompt: The same illuminated parchment leaf, sepia ink with muted gold-red-blue wash, single gilt border rule, and no lettering anywhere on the page except the small roman-capital titles beneath each medallion. The page is divided top to bottom into two parallel columns separated by a plain gold vertical rule but without any header text, each column opening with the medallion already shown in the overview for this part. Left column, from top: RICHMANN'S LEGENDARY BALL, 1753 (an engraving-style scene of a man struck by a dramatic fiery sphere), joined by a gold thread down to D-CY'S WHIRLING FIREBALL (a man on a rainy road confronted by a small whirling barrel-shaped fireball). Right column, from top, aligned beside it: DORSTONE'S BOILING TUB, 1936 (a red-hot ball falling toward a wash-tub beneath a cottage window), then FIERY BALL IN THE GLASS DOOR (a woman in a car watching a glowing yellow-flamed ball in her front-door glass), then 33 CM BALL FROM TRIGGERED LIGHTNING (researchers at a test ground watching a ball of light flare from a lightning-struck steel plate), then SPECTRUM OF THE QINGHAI BALL (two cameras on a hillside recording a glowing ball above a power-line tower at night). Thin gold threads run down each column in sequence. Near the foot of the page, a thread from the bottom of the left column (D-CY'S WHIRLING FIREBALL) and a thread from the bottom of the right column (SPECTRUM OF THE QINGHAI BALL) both bend inward and meet at a single final medallion centred at the very bottom: BUILDING THE SHARED DATABASE, showing robed scholars at a table laying a road-sketch and a spectrograph record side by side into one open ledger. questions.question: What does it mean for the field's maturity that a lightning handbook finds 2400 ball lightning references "puzzling" against 6000 for all lightning topics?

passages.quote: The authors were puzzled by 2400 references in Stenhoff’s book (1999), whereas their handbook on all lightning aspects comprises over 6000.

questions.question: Given how little instrumental evidence exists for ball lightning, why focus specifically on reports from scientists and trained professionals?

passages.quote: Rakov and Uman (2003, p. 656, p. 658) characterized ball lightning as “a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings.”
Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals.

questions.question: If the author admits the case collection is incomplete, how much weight can its conclusions carry?

passages.quote: it does not claim to be complete but can and will be expanded by forthcoming reports in the future.
Scientists who read the article and who have not reported their experience are invited to share it with the author.

questions.question: Why bring up famous physicists' secondhand ball lightning stories at all, if they turn out to lack any real data?

passages.quote: Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data

questions.question: Why count childhood sightings by people who only later became scientists, if they had no scientific training at the time of the observation?

passages.quote: It can be argued that all children have similar observation capabilities. However, scientific training and profession might improve the quality of their recalled eyewitness testimony.

questions.question: If weather stations are being automated and losing human observers, what does that mean for collecting future high-quality sightings?

passages.quote: it eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena such as ball lightning. Whether this will be compensated by citizen science and the spread of mobile phone and web cameras remains uncertain.

questions.question: If the cases vary so widely in size, duration, and behavior, can they really all be instances of one single phenomenon?

passages.quote: and some outliers are hard to integrate into one general ball lightning model. This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning.

questions.question: Doesn't exposing Richmann's famous death as ordinary lightning, not a ball lightning strike, undercut trust in other oft-cited classic cases?

passages.quote: From an investigation protocol with autopsy results (Anonymous, 1755, pp. 64–68), it is obvious that it was a conventional lightning accident caused by a non-grounded conductor.

questions.question: If researchers who triggered lightning-induced glowing effects in the field refuse to call them ball lightning, what does that say about ever confirming the phenomenon in a lab?

passages.quote: Uman and colleagues call what was produced not ball lightning but point to interesting effects of different materials under the influence of lightning.

questions.question: What does the article say the term "ball lightning" refers to?
questions.referenceAnswer: It refers to a still-unexplained group of short-lived, glowing phenomena in atmospheric electricity that appear seemingly at random in time and place, last only a few seconds, and then vanish, sometimes leaving traces and sometimes not.

evidence.quote: stands for a still unexplained group of metastable luminous phenomena in atmospheric electricity. Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without.

questions.question: Why does most of the collected material on ball lightning remain anecdotal rather than scientifically documented?
questions.premise: Ball lightning appears unpredictably and lasts only a few seconds.
questions.referenceAnswer: Because of its unpredictable occurrence in time and place, it is very hard to capture with instruments, so most of what exists is eyewitness testimony rather than recordings or measurements.

evidence.quote: Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.

questions.question: According to Rakov and Uman's 2003 lightning handbook, what is missing despite almost 5000 collected observation reports of ball lightning?
questions.referenceAnswer: Scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings is largely missing, even though witness reports are numerous.

evidence.quote: a phenomenon for which there exists numerous witness reports but little, if any, scientific documentation such as photographs, videotapes, or other scientific recordings.

questions.question: Why did earlier researchers like Singer and Stenhoff pay special attention to reports from scientists and trained professionals specifically?
questions.premise: Rakov and Uman note that ball lightning has thousands of witness reports but almost no scientific documentation.
questions.referenceAnswer: Because direct instrumental monitoring of the phenomenon is extremely rare, so reports from scientifically trained observers were treated as a more reliable source of evidence than ordinary eyewitness accounts.

evidence.quote: Therefore, Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals.

questions.question: How many total cases does this review compile, and over what countries and years?
questions.referenceAnswer: It compiles 41 cases from eight countries, spanning the years 1868 to 2020.

evidence.quote: Forty-one cases from eight countries, 1868–2020, are presented in abstract form with a synthesis.

questions.question: Of these 41 cases, how many came from previously published sources, from the author's own records, and from a Russian database?
questions.premise: The review compiles 41 cases from eight countries spanning 1868 to 2020.
questions.referenceAnswer: Twenty were previously published case histories, fifteen came from the author's own work, and six came from a Russian database.

evidence.quote: the review compiles 20 published case histories, adds 15 from the author’s work and six from a Russian database.

questions.question: In physicist Walther Gerlach's 1927 Tübingen observation, what surprising calculation did he make about the ball lightning's speed and sound?
questions.referenceAnswer: He calculated the ball travelled at roughly 1200 m/s, about Mach 3.6, yet it was observed moving silently without producing the sonic boom such a speed should cause.

evidence.quote: His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom).

questions.question: What physical evidence let astrophysicist Axel Wittmann calculate an energy density for the fireball fragments he saw as a child in 1951?
questions.referenceAnswer: The smaller spheres that fell from the main fireball left circular patches of melted asphalt on the wet road, and using the melting point of the asphalt's bitumen and the water layer, he calculated an energy density of at least about 1.9 × 10^7 joules per cubic metre.

evidence.quote: Wittmann “calculated the energy density of the plasma spheres to be at least 1.9 × 10⁷ J m−3” (Wittmann, 1971, 625).

questions.question: What did atmospheric chemist Dmitriev find when he took air samples after a 1965 ball lightning event near river rafts in Russia?
questions.referenceAnswer: The air samples contained ozone and nitrogen dioxide at concentrations 50 to 100 times higher than in normal air.

evidence.quote: The samples contained a maximum of 1.3 mg m−3 ozone (O₃) and 1.6 mg m−3 nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), which was 50–100 times higher than in normal air

questions.question: In the statistical synopsis of the 41 cases, what percentage occurred within an ongoing thunderstorm, and what percentage showed no connection to a thunderstorm at all?
questions.referenceAnswer: 73% occurred within a thunderstorm, while 17% showed no connection to a thunderstorm.

evidence.quote: 73 % occurred within thunderstorms, 10 % before or after, and 17 % without a connection.

questions.question: Across the cases with reported sizes and durations, what range of object sizes and observation durations did the synopsis find?
questions.referenceAnswer: Reported sizes ranged from 1.5 cm to 15 m, with most under 20 cm, while durations ranged from 1.5 to 180 seconds, with most lasting under 3 seconds.

evidence.quote: Reported object sizes (28 cases) range from 1.5 cm to 15 m, with the maximum below 20 cm and several cases over 1 m.
Reported observation durations (25 cases) range from 1.5 to 180 s with the maximum under 3 s but 5–6 cases in the higher categories.

questions.question: Given this variety, what conclusion does the author draw about trying to define one strict "ball lightning norm"?
questions.premise: Reported sizes and durations varied enormously across the cases, from under 20 cm to 15 m and from under 3 seconds to 180 seconds.
questions.referenceAnswer: He argues it would be epistemologically odd to define a single "ball lightning norm" and automatically exclude cases that do not fit it, noting that some researchers instead suggest there may be more than one type of ball lightning.

evidence.quote: Epistemologically, it would be odd to define a “ball lightning norm” and a priori exclude cases that do not meet this definition.
There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated

questions.question: What does the article reveal about the true cause of physicist Georg Wilhelm Richmann's famous 1753 death, long cited as a ball lightning case?
questions.referenceAnswer: Investigation records with autopsy results show he was actually killed by a conventional lightning strike through an ungrounded conductor, not by true ball lightning, although a popular engraving falsely showed a lightning ball hitting him.

evidence.quote: it is obvious that it was a conventional lightning accident caused by a non-grounded conductor. However, a popular engraving pictured a lightning ball that hit Richmann.

questions.question: What does the author suggest this myth reveals about ball lightning's popular image?
questions.premise: Richmann's famous death, long linked to ball lightning imagery, was actually caused by ordinary lightning rather than a verified ball lightning encounter.
questions.referenceAnswer: He suggests ball lightning acquired a deadly, destructive popular image partly fed by injuries and damage actually caused by ordinary cloud-to-ground lightning strikes rather than genuine ball lightning events.

evidence.quote: Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.

questions.question: What physical evidence allowed researchers to estimate the energy involved in the widely cited 1936 Dorstone case, where a fireball was said to have fallen into a tub of water?
questions.referenceAnswer: Using the reported amount of water in the tub and the fact that it boiled afterward, researchers calculated that the ball would have needed an energy density of at least about 2000 joules per cubic centimetre.

evidence.quote: the calculations found that at least 2 × 10³ J cm−3 would be involved (Barry, 1980).

questions.question: What did the spectroscopic video recording of the 2012 Qinghai Plateau ball lightning event in China reveal about a possible explanation for its formation?
questions.referenceAnswer: The recorded spectrum showed lines from iron, calcium, silicon, nitrogen, and oxygen, consistent with a theory that ball lightning can form when a lightning strike vaporizes material from the soil.

evidence.quote: The ball lightning spectrum showed lines due to Fe, CA, Si, N, and O consistent with the Abrahamson and Dinniss (2002) soil strike theory.

questions.question: How does the author describe the overall state of ball lightning research, borrowing a term from Turner?
questions.referenceAnswer: He describes it as a "fragmented science," carried out mostly part-time and by individuals working separately—some collecting data, some building theories, some running laboratory tests—without good coordination between them.

evidence.quote: Turner called ball lightning research a “fragmented science” (2001).
Most ball lightning research was (and still is) part-time and individualized – some people collecting data, some theorizing, some doing laboratory tests.

questions.question: What does the author see as the key to overcoming this fragmentation and advancing the field going forward?
questions.premise: Ball lightning research has long been fragmented, carried out piecemeal by individuals rather than coordinated teams.
questions.referenceAnswer: He is optimistic that progress will be faster with better-coordinated international research, using well-documented physical-evidence cases as benchmarks alongside growing mobile phone and webcam footage, to build a systematic database against which ball lightning theories can be tested.

evidence.quote: systematic multidisciplinary case documentation and discussion can lead to a database against which ball lightning theories and simulations can be critically assessed.

questions.question: What invitation does the author extend to scientists who have personally witnessed ball lightning but never reported it?
questions.referenceAnswer: He invites them to share their experience with him, so it can be added to the growing collection of documented cases.

evidence.quote: Scientists who read the article and who have not reported their experience are invited to share it with the author.

ideas.name: Who gets observed shapes what gets measured
ideas.statement: The kind of person doing the observing, and how that group of observers came to be selected, can systematically shift the reported size, duration, and other features of an event, so a difference between two observer groups' statistics can reflect reporting bias rather than a real difference in the phenomenon.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: The comparison between the scientist sample's sizes and durations and the general-public databases' figures is only meaningful as a finding if differing observer selection can itself shape the numbers; otherwise the comparison is just two unrelated tallies placed side by side.
ideas.analogy: It is like comparing average fish-size estimates from scuba divers with tape measures against estimates from anglers telling stories at the dock: the gap tells you as much about who is doing the measuring as about the fish.

occurrences.quote: Reported object sizes (28 cases) range from 1.5 cm to 15 m, with the maximum below 20 cm and several cases over 1 m. Compared to 405 ball lightning cases from Austrian and German databases (Keul and Stummer, 2002), the scientists’ size distribution is left skewed.
occurrences.reasoning: Presents a skew between observer groups as a noteworthy result, which only has meaning if observer type can bias the measured distribution.

occurrences.quote: Reported observation durations (25 cases) range from 1.5 to 180 s with the maximum under 3 s but 5–6 cases in the higher categories. Mean is 19.5 s, standard deviation is 38.6, median is 4.0, and mode of 2.5 s. The 405 ball lightning cases, 2002, had lower means (7.7–15.4 s), median of 3–5, mode of 2–5, and range of 1–900 s.
occurrences.reasoning: Juxtaposes duration statistics from two differently-selected samples as if the comparison itself were informative about reporting rather than only about the phenomenon.

ideas.name: Trained observers count more than lay witnesses
ideas.statement: When a phenomenon cannot be captured instrumentally, the testimony of people with scientific or technical training (physicists, engineers, weather observers, coastguards) deserves special weight compared with ordinary public reports, because their training should make their descriptions more precise and reliable.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: The whole project of compiling scientists' and professionals' accounts only makes sense if this kind of witness is assumed to give better data than the general public; otherwise there would be no reason to single them out.

occurrences.quote: As chances to monitor this transient phenomenon are low, it seems promising to evaluate observation reports by scientists and trained professionals.
occurrences.reasoning: States outright that expert witnesses are worth specially seeking out.

occurrences.quote: Therefore, Singer (1971, chap. 5.B.2) and Stenhoff (1999, chap. 10.4) paid special attention to ball lightning reports coming from scientists or trained professionals.
occurrences.reasoning: Shows prior researchers already acting on the premise that expert witnesses merit separate treatment.

occurrences.quote: It can be argued that all children have similar observation capabilities. However, scientific training and profession might improve the quality of their recalled eyewitness testimony.
occurrences.reasoning: Explicitly claims that professional training upgrades the value of a recollection, justifying inclusion of childhood memories of future scientists.

ideas.name: Popular imagery can distort a phenomenon's record
ideas.statement: A dramatic image or story that captures public imagination can get permanently attached to a phenomenon's reputation, even when the underlying event was something ordinary, and this distorts how the phenomenon is remembered and studied afterward.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this idea, bringing up Richmann's death, which was an ordinary lightning strike, inside a history of ball lightning would be a non sequitur rather than an illustration of how a false popular image attached itself to the subject.

occurrences.quote: However, a popular engraving pictured a lightning ball that hit Richmann.
occurrences.reasoning: Shows a popular image creating a false association between an ordinary fatal lightning strike and ball lightning specifically.

occurrences.quote: Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.
occurrences.reasoning: States directly that the phenomenon's popular reputation was shaped by conflation with unrelated ordinary events.

occurrences.quote: Here, everyday life theories or mindsets are more influential than science.
occurrences.reasoning: Generalizes the point that public narrative, not scientific finding, often governs how such a phenomenon is understood.

ideas.name: Uncoordinated individual effort fragments a field
ideas.statement: A research topic can remain permanently unresolved not for lack of data or ideas but because the people collecting data, the people building theories, and the people running experiments work separately and are never organized into one coordinated effort.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this idea, the catalogue of scattered monographs, unpublished reports, and private databases would read as mere history rather than as a diagnosis of why ball lightning has stayed unsolved for nearly two centuries.
ideas.analogy: It is like a construction site where one crew pours a foundation, another draws blueprints, and a third tests materials, but none of them are working from the same plan or on the same building.

occurrences.quote: For the same reason, Turner called ball lightning research a "fragmented science" (2001).
occurrences.reasoning: Names the disorganization itself as the diagnosis for the field's lack of progress.

occurrences.quote: Most ball lightning research was (and still is) part-time and individualized – some people collecting data, some theorizing, some doing laboratory tests.
occurrences.reasoning: Attributes the field's stagnation to separation of roles rather than to any lack of effort or evidence.

occurrences.quote: Nevertheless, the author is still optimistic that scientific progress will be faster when capacities are better coordinated.
occurrences.reasoning: The proposed remedy (coordination) only makes sense if fragmentation, not scarcity of data, is the real obstacle.

ideas.name: One name may cover several distinct phenomena
ideas.statement: Reports gathered under a single label may actually describe more than one physically distinct kind of event, each with its own mechanism, rather than one phenomenon that a single theory must explain.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without entertaining this possibility, the wide spread of sizes, durations, and behaviours in the case collection would look like a failure of observation or theory rather than a hint that 'ball lightning' might not be one single thing.

occurrences.quote: There may be more than one type of ball lightning and more than one mechanism by which ball lightning is generated
occurrences.reasoning: States directly that the category might not correspond to a single underlying mechanism.

occurrences.quote: This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning.
occurrences.reasoning: Connects the sample's outlier cases directly to the multiple-types hypothesis as a way of accommodating them.

ideas.name: Lightning-network data as an independent check
ideas.statement: Automated lightning-detection networks that record the time, location, polarity, and current of ordinary strokes can be cross-referenced against eyewitness reports of an unrelated phenomenon to give those reports a kind of instrumental backing they otherwise lack.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this idea, citing a precise stroke current and distance alongside a witness's story would be an odd non sequitur rather than a way of partially objectifying an otherwise pure testimony.

occurrences.quote: The upswing of modern lightning location networks (like BLIDS, German lightning information service, or ALDIS, Austrian lightning detection and information system) opened up new options, so recently, a first correlation of 34 central European ball lightning events, 1994–2016, with lightning location data was done together with ALDIS (Keul and Diendorfer, 2018).
occurrences.reasoning: Frames instrumental lightning records as a new resource for validating otherwise unverifiable eyewitness cases.

occurrences.quote: ALDIS recorded 10 lightning events during 22:01–22:28 LT for 5 km around Neueßling. At 22:16:28 LT, a strong positive cloud–ground stroke with +170.4 kA happened 0.5 km west in the back of the witnesses.
occurrences.reasoning: Uses an automated network's precise record as corroborating detail for a witness's account.

ideas.name: Independent witnesses corroborate reality
ideas.statement: When several people, in different places or at different moments, independently report seeing closely matching objects, that convergence is treated as evidence the phenomenon was really there rather than a private perceptual or psychological event.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this idea, the repeated emphasis on how many separate observers saw a given ball, or how similar successive events looked, would be pointless detail rather than evidence strengthening the case.

occurrences.quote: So we get a 1868 multiple object event with sightings from three inner Vienna districts, Landstrasse, Mariahilf, and Neubau, in a triangle 3.4–1.3–3 km apart, with two similar objects (colour, size, rays) and a different one.
occurrences.reasoning: Treats agreement among three separately located witnesses as itself a notable, evidential fact.

occurrences.quote: At around 18:30 and 18:50, two more events occurred (Mathias, 1916) in the same shape and procedure as the first one.
occurrences.reasoning: Repetition of the same pattern across witnesses and times is reported as reinforcing the case rather than as coincidence.

occurrences.quote: Among several close cloud–ground flashes, one near the Bragg building caused ball lightning which was noticed by several staff members from the Mott building as a bright object, "luminous haze", and as stationary blue-white light. Three more observers saw a ball moving over the ground, bright blue-white light, visible for 4–5 s.
occurrences.reasoning: Multiple independent sightings of the same event are stacked up as corroboration.

ideas.name: Leftover damage lets you calculate an unmeasured event
ideas.statement: Even without direct instruments trained on a transient event, the physical changes it leaves behind (melted material, boiled water, timing of sounds) can be used after the fact to back-calculate quantities like its energy content or speed.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without this idea, the melted-asphalt, boiled-water-tub, and thunder-timing passages would just be colourful anecdotes rather than attempts to pin a number on an unphotographed phenomenon.
ideas.analogy: It is like a fire investigator inferring how hot a blaze burned from which metal fittings melted and which did not, without ever having pointed a thermometer at the flames.

occurrences.quote: Taking into account water layer and the melting point of B-80 bitumen, Wittmann "calculated the energy density of the plasma spheres to be at least 1.9 × 10⁷ J m−3"
occurrences.reasoning: Derives a physical quantity for an unmeasured event purely from the state of melted asphalt it left behind.

occurrences.quote: With different ball diameters, an assumed amount of four gallons (18 L) of water, and a temperature rise from 10–20 to 60 °C, the calculations found that at least 2 × 10³ J cm−3 would be involved (Barry, 1980).
occurrences.reasoning: Reconstructs an energy estimate for the Dorstone ball purely from the boiled water it left behind, with no direct measurement of the object.

occurrences.quote: Gerlach did his calculations: with a speed of sound of 330 m s−1 and observed times of the lightning’s thunder and the explosion, he got a ball lightning trajectory of 1300 + 1150 = 2450 m.
occurrences.reasoning: Infers the object's trajectory and speed from timing of sounds rather than from watching its motion directly.

ideas.name: Shock injury and fright trauma are separable
ideas.statement: A person struck by an electrical discharge can suffer two different and separable conditions: an immediate physical/neurological injury from the current itself, and a distinct, longer-lasting psychological disturbance caused by the fright, which should not be confused with each other.
ideas.whyYouNeedIt: Without distinguishing these two effects, the case of the frightened, limping, babbling patient would look like a single mysterious illness rather than two linked but different consequences of the same event.

occurrences.quote: He distinguished the short-lived neurological effects (keraunoparalysis) from a
occurrences.reasoning: Marks the split between a physical electrical injury and something else as the key diagnostic move.

occurrences.quote: long-lived traumatic neurosis (skin anaesthesia, motor paralysis, sensory losses, thunderstorm phobia, etc.)
occurrences.reasoning: Names the second, purely psychological condition that must be told apart from the electrical injury to make sense of the patient's lingering symptoms.

occurrences.quote: Charcot’s discrimination between keraunoparalysis and neuropsychological aftereffects is still made in medicine (Andrews et al., 2017).
occurrences.reasoning: Confirms this is a durable, general distinction being introduced, not just a one-off diagnosis.

quotes.text: With thousands of eyewitness reports, but few instrumental records and no consensus about a theory, ball lightning remains an unsolved problem in atmospheric physics.
quotes.reason: States the central puzzle the whole article is built around.

quotes.text: It is concluded that well-documented cases from trained observers can promote fieldwork and stimulate and evaluate ball lightning theories.
quotes.reason: The paper's main conclusion stated in its own words.

quotes.text: Ball lightning appears seemingly random in time and space, lasts a few seconds, and disappears with traces or without. Because of its unpredictable occurrence, most of the collected material remains anecdotal.
quotes.reason: Explains why the phenomenon is so hard to study scientifically.

quotes.text: Ball lightning cases also have a psychological side, when it comes to eyewitness quality, (non-)reporting, and public and media event labelling. Here, everyday life theories or mindsets are more influential than science.
quotes.reason: Flags the human/psychological complication running through the whole review.

quotes.text: Several alleged observations (e.g. of Niels Bohr and Victor Weisskopf), often quoted in science or popular journals, were incorrect or lacked data: Tuck (1971) only wrote that he heard from Weisskopf that Bohr had once seen ball lightning.
quotes.reason: Shows the author's critical filtering of famous but unreliable anecdotes.

quotes.text: His speed calculation of 1225 m s−1 is quite amazing, because it means the object travelled at a speed of Mach 3.6 “soundless”, without an acoustic effect (sonic boom). This is one of the rare occasions where ball lightning met a gifted experimental physicist.
quotes.reason: Highlights one of the most physically puzzling details in the whole collection of cases.

quotes.text: A special category of reports is ball lightning encountered by children who, in their later life, followed a scientific career and then described in detail what they saw. It can be argued that all children have similar observation capabilities. However, scientific training and profession might improve the quality of their recalled eyewitness testimony.
quotes.reason: Introduces and justifies a distinct, carefully reasoned category of evidence.

quotes.text: The tendency of weather services to do without observers and automate synoptic stations (including German mountaintop observatories) may be justified from an economic standpoint, but it eliminates high-quality observations of rare phenomena such as ball lightning. Whether this will be compensated by citizen science and the spread of mobile phone and web cameras remains uncertain.
quotes.reason: A concrete worry about the future supply of good evidence, linking past methods to present uncertainty.

quotes.text: Thus, even this relatively small sample of educated and trained observers shows a variety of situations, object sizes, and case durations, and some outliers are hard to integrate into one general ball lightning model. This has led some researchers (as Rakov and Uman, 2003) to assume several types of ball lightning.
quotes.reason: The key finding of the statistical synthesis section.

quotes.text: Epistemologically, it would be odd to define a “ball lightning norm” and a priori exclude cases that do not meet this definition. Regardless of all problems with an explanatory theory, detailed case reports should be documented.
quotes.reason: States the author's methodological stance against prematurely narrowing what counts as a valid case.

quotes.text: As in the 1818 Frankenstein novel, the grim fate of an avantgarde scientist sounded plausible. Ball lightning acquired a deadly and destructive popular image fed by injuries and damage caused by ordinary cloud–ground strokes.
quotes.reason: Explains how a famous misattributed death shaped the popular myth of ball lightning.

quotes.text: The main difference between modern science and Frankenstein’s laboratory is guiding research paradigms that – in the case of natural phenomena – condition a proper order of systematic data acquisition, formation, and testing of hypotheses and theories, and – if possible – laboratory simulation.
quotes.reason: A sharp framing of what separates rigorous science from the popular myth evoked earlier.

quotes.text: In the case of ball lightning, the research logic is distorted by a random phenomenon that is hard to observe, irreproducible, and mostly reported by change. Weird popular press stories and a lack of economic (except some military) interest did not encourage scientific community nor weather services to deal with this “unsolved problem in atmospheric physics” (Stenhoff, 1999).
quotes.reason: Summarizes why the field has stayed fragmented for so long.

quotes.text: Most ball lightning research was (and still is) part-time and individualized – some people collecting data, some theorizing, some doing laboratory tests.
quotes.reason: Captures the disorganized state of the field the author wants to fix.

quotes.text: Nevertheless, the author is still optimistic that scientific progress will be faster when capacities are better coordinated.
quotes.reason: The author's closing note of hope, setting up the call to action.

entries.name: COST Action P18
entries.background: COST Action P18 was a European collaborative research programme bringing together roughly 30 researchers to study the physics of lightning, including unresolved questions like ball lightning.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A US network of automated sky cameras set up to photograph meteors and track falling meteorites across many states, whose decade of continuous images were later searched for possible ball-lightning captures.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.background: BLIDS is a German network of ground sensors that detects and locates lightning strikes across the country in real time, recording details such as timing, position, and current strength.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.background: ALDIS is Austria's equivalent lightning-detection network, used to pinpoint where and when strokes occur and to measure their electrical polarity and strength.

entries.name: Cloud–ground stroke
entries.senseHere: A lightning discharge that travels between a cloud and the ground, as opposed to one that stays within or between clouds; the article tallies how many ball-lightning sightings coincided with each kind.

entries.name: Positive and negative lightning strokes
entries.senseHere: Lightning strokes are classed by the direction their electric charge flows, measured as peak current in kiloamps; the article notes an unusually high share of positive strokes linked to ball-lightning sightings.

entries.name: Pyotr Leonidovich Kapitsa
entries.background: A Soviet physicist and Nobel laureate known for low-temperature physics, who also proposed a theoretical explanation for how ball lightning might form and sustain itself.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: An Austrian geologist and mineralogist at the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna, whose detailed 1868 report and sketch of a ball-lightning sighting is one of the earliest scientific accounts in the article.

entries.name: Angular diameter
entries.senseHere: The apparent size of an object measured as an angle across the sky rather than its true physical size, used by witnesses like Haidinger and Wilhelm to later calculate the object's real diameter once its distance is known.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: A German physicist famous for the Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrating quantum spin, who also reported and mathematically analyzed his own 1927 ball-lightning sighting.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: A British radio astronomer, later a professor of physical electronics, whose widely publicized 1963 account of ball lightning on an aircraft became one of the most cited sightings in the field.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: A Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who was killed in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity, an incident later mythologized as a ball-lightning death.

entries.name: Keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A short-lived paralysis or numbness in a limb caused by a nearby lightning strike or an encounter with ball lightning, as distinct from longer-lasting nerve or psychological damage.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: A pioneering French neurologist at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris and teacher of Sigmund Freud, known for studying the nervous aftereffects of trauma, including lightning-related injuries.

entries.name: Triggered lightning
entries.senseHere: Lightning deliberately set off for research by launching a small rocket trailing a thin grounded wire into a storm cloud, letting scientists study strikes under controlled conditions.

entries.name: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.background: This theory proposes that when lightning hits soil, it vaporizes minerals into a cloud of tiny burning particles that can hover and glow, producing what looks like a ball of fire.

entries.name: Slitless spectroscopy
entries.senseHere: A method of capturing the color spectrum of a light source directly on video using a diffraction grating instead of a narrow slit, letting researchers identify the chemical elements glowing in a ball-lightning event.

entries.name: "Fragmented science"
entries.background: A phrase coined by researcher Turner in 2001 to describe how ball-lightning research has scattered into many disconnected theories, observers, and laboratory experiments without a unifying framework.

events.label: Durward's son struck at Loch Tummel

events.label: Morris's ball lands in water tub, Dorstone

events.label: Durward's flying-boat encounter en route to Iraq

occurrences.quote: James Durward, a British military meteorologist, 1936–1940 director of the Iraq Meteorological Service (Anonymous, 1956), encountered ball lightning on his flight to Iraq in summer 1938.

events.label: Nikitin's childhood sighting at Belaya Glina

occurrences.quote: In mid-August 1948, about 20:00 LT, in Belaya Glina, northwest of Krasnodar, south Russia, “I walked along a village street . . . on a hot summer day without rain.”

events.label: Wittmann's childhood sighting, Neustadt bei Coburg

occurrences.quote: Alexander E. Mickelson, doctor of technical sciences, was in a cottage house 17 km from Riga, Latvia, on 7 June 1967, with distant lightning flashes outside but no rain.

events.label: Dunford's sighting at Rutherford Appleton Lab

occurrences.quote: Eric Dunford, space scientist at the Rutherford Appleton Laboratory, between Harwell and Chilton, Oxfordshire, UK, saw ball lightning with his wife and another person on 18 April 1968, at about 19:15–19:30 LT during a thunderstorm with heavy rain.

events.label: Geiswinkler's ball crosses villa room, Wörthersee

entries.text: Ball lightning has thousands of eyewitness accounts but no agreed theory, and this paper sets out to add scientist testimony to that record.
The name existed before any real consensus formed, leaving a huge literature that still could not settle what ball lightning is.
Since direct recordings are nearly impossible, this review turns to trained observers' testimony as the next best evidence.
These firsthand professional accounts supply the detailed, varied raw material the methodology promised, without yet resolving what unites them.
Beyond laboratory-trained scientists, ordinary duty-bound observers extend the same body of testimony and its unresolved puzzle.
Tallying all these accounts exposes just how little the sightings agree on, undercutting hope for one single explanation.
Where witness memory falls short, a few cases with physical traces or instruments offer the firmer evidence the field has lacked.
Having gathered testimony and physical benchmarks alike, the case is made for pooling them systematically rather than working alone.
The underlying case material is opened to further use, leaving the theoretical question exactly as unsettled as it began.
